Definition: from G1 (as a negative particle) and G5424; properly, mindless, i.e. stupid, (by implication) ignorant, (specially) egotistic, (practically) rash, or (morally) unbelieving:--fool(-ish), unwise.
BiblicalUsage: Paul calls the man who doubts the resurrection a fool in 1 Corinthians 15:36 — ‘thou fool, that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die’ — because the seed in the ground already teaches what he denies. Jesus uses the same word for the rich man in Luke 12:20, whose soul is required of him the very night his barns are full, and Paul turns it into a command in Ephesians 5:17: be not unwise, but understand what the will of the Lord is. Romans 2:20 shows the other side, the Jew who claims to be an instructor of the foolish while holding only the form of knowledge.
TheologicalSignificance: I hold that foolishness in Scripture is never about being slow; it is about living as though God will not call the account. The fool sows nothing, plans for decades he does not have, and teaches others from a form of truth he never obeyed. Wisdom, by contrast, is simply understanding what the Lord wills — and doing it while there is still time.
Sources: Strong's Exhaustive Concordance (1890), via OpenScriptures Strong's Dictionary (CC BY-SA)
